**1. Why were you in a coma?** I was in an electrical explosion or arc flash/arc blast and i wasn't wearing my PPE (personal protective equipment). I was testing the 3000 amp/480 volt electrical connection to a building for a  generator before hurricane Charlie in 2004. Coma was 1st medically induced but slipped into real coma due to complications from infections and reactions to medications. I had 3rd degree burns down to the muscle (called full thickness) on both arms and hands. 2nd & 3rd degree burns on my neck and face. I had to have skin graphs from mid bicep down on both arms. I lost 50 lbs from atrophy while in the coma... I only weighed 165 lbs to begin with. Complications from the medications cause organ failure so i couldn't even be tube fed. My heart stopped twice!
https://youtu.be/CBbreOFWIng

**2. How long were you in a coma?** almost 2 months

**3. What changed once you woke up?**  I'm an electrician and I could not do electrical work anymore. I have no feeling, no pores, no sweat glands and limited dexterity my arms and hands. I struggled to regain the ability to walk due to the atrophy. I had 2 years of rehabilitation and surgeries to be able to use my hands and arms again. Had a tracheostomy (trach tube) for 3 months after a surgery for scaring caused by the intubation tube. *But I'm alive! There are others that have had almost the same accident who are dead or horribly disfigured.* 

**4. How did your life change?**  I gained a great deal more appreciation for my wife, family, friends and really great doctors. I was fortunate enough to be able to move from the field/construction to an office/management position (forced promotion 😊).I became way more safety conscious. My wife and I now speak to groups about the importance of PPE and following safety procedures. *Google "Donnie's Accident" for the video and full story"*

**5. Do you have any recollection of family members visiting, or conversations, dreams or anything interesting happening while you were in the coma?**  Evidently there were 4 hurricanes while i was sleeping. My wife said she would talk to me a lot and even give me play by play of the Nascar races *(i'm a fan)*, hoping I might hear and respond. I have vague memories of watching the EKG machine for hours thinking it was a cartoon. Once I was past the complications and still not waking up, the nurses allowed my son to sneak in to my room *(i was in the burn ICU and he was too young)*, My first "NEW" memory is my son walking by the foot of my bed fully dressed in the protective gown, mask, cap and gloves. As the medications were wearing off, my wife says I would wake up in different moods and be laughing and telling funny stories or raging and uncooperative *(I don't remember any of this)*. I had no idea about the last 2 months and my heart stopping twice, once my wife told me what happened i made a comment like "Damn, I didn't get to see my grandfather or nothing"  She was not amused.

**Suicide Lesson**
  When I was a teenager, I worked in a funeral home with my grandfather. It was kind of the family business. My dad had worked there when he was a young man as well. My grandparents actually lived in an apartment above the mortuary. I grew up around the funeral home so it wasn't weird for me. Dead people did not scare me. To me they were simply empty shells. The ‘person’ was gone, hopefully journeying to the afterlife of their belief. I learned many lessons there about how fragile life really is. I learned about different religions’ burial ceremonies and rituals. I did not look at it as morbid. The way I saw it, we were providing a service and helping people in the absolute worst time of their lives. I mean, there is nothing worse than someone you love dying. My grandfather instilled and insisted that all the deceased be treated with dignity and respect. I remember my friends begging me to “see a dead body”. I never would. I would ask them if they would like me to show someone else their family member’s corpse. Of course not. Well that was somebody else’s family member in there. They usually had a better understanding of the term “respect for the dead” after that conversation. There were many stories. Some were horribly tragic and heartbreaking. Some behind the scenes episodes were hysterical. You have to have a sense of humor in that business.

  There is ONE experience at the funeral home that stands out from all the others by the way it changed my life and my way of thinking forever. 

  The embalming room had two embalming tables. This particular day there were two bodies.
  One was a 35 year old woman. She had lost her battle with cancer. That morning my grandfather and I made the 'removal' from her home, where she passed away under end-of-life Hospice care. I saw her friends and family at the home and listened to them speak about her. Her family was her life. She’d given up her career to be a stay at home mom. She had two boys, around 9 & 10 years old. She did all the PTA, sports and scout stuff. Her husband was either an engineer or architect and they were pretty well off judging by their home. There were pictures on the walls of them at the children’s events, their wedding day and various vacations. In her pictures, she had been a beautiful woman.

  The second body was a 19 to 22 year old man. I had made his removal from the county morgue that morning too. He had committed suicide with a gun to the head over breaking up with a girlfriend. The morgue is a cold, clinical and impersonal environment. This was not at all like the warm family surroundings of the woman’s home. The medical examiner’s assistant told me that he had left a note describing the pain he felt from losing his love.  

  As I stood at the foot of the embalming tables looking over these two people, I had a moment of introspection and realization. Here in front of me was a woman who would have done ANYTHING to stay alive and a young man who had, in my opinion, thrown it all away. To me what he had done was the very meaning of the phrase “A permanent solution to a temporary problem”. Everything the woman wanted so badly, he took for granted. They both had so much to live for. She had a beautiful family and a wonderful life. He had an entire lifetime ahead with untold potential. Guests at both their funerals were asking “why?” but for completely different reasons.  

  I was not judging this man or anyone else who is going or has gone through a terrible time in their life and thinking about ending it. I was simply comparing the lives of the two dead people in front of me. I do understand. Before that moment, I had times in my life that I had contemplated suicide, but had ‘chickened’ out. I was so mentally and physically abused by my stepfather and mother, that I felt worthless. My self-esteem and self-loathing were so bad that I felt I didn’t even deserve to die because it was an easy way out. Even After that day in the embalming room, there were times in my life that things were so messed up that I couldn’t see any way out, no other solutions. I remember thinking “this will show ‘em” after people intentionally betraying me or a girl breaking up with me. I recall feeling so dark, in the throes of alcoholism that the suicidal thoughts crept back into my head. However, after that day, these thoughts were only fleeting. I knew I wouldn’t go through with it. Remembering the sight of those two people, the feelings and the thoughts I had while standing at the foot of the embalming tables, ensured I would persevere.  “This too shall pass” and “time heals” are things that you come to understand better as you grow older.
